al - Bashir

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As international condemnation floods in about the al-Bashir incident, we ask if government's blatant disregard of a high court order is the first step to a full blown constitutional crisis.

Summary:
With the South African government seemingly complicit in allowing a high profile fugitive from justice to escape our borders, we examine the consequences of the ruling party's decision to blatantly disregard both international and local laws. In the meantime, reports are circulating that SA troops were basically threatened and or held hostage in Sudan during al-Bashir's visit to SA. But should the interests of SA's relationships with it's African counterparts trump the rule of law?

The government wants to kill all the blacks, and replace them with Arabs, because Darfur land is good for cultivation.” Is this widely known and accurate? Can we confirm govt policy to kill the blacks? Graham: it’s accurate in that the genocide has been about this… and is the basis of his ICC indictment Arab military George doesn’t want this out…

3. He wants Pierre De Vos and to take out some of Angela – three times at least Angela appears too much rather use more of Pierre
4. The Israeli comment mustn’t be split in two let Gwede say it in full and don’t interrupt him with Angela

Script:


Sound Up Judge Dunston Mlambo
…The conduct of the respondents to the extent that they have failed to take steps to arrest and or detain the president of the Republic of Sudan, Omar Hassan Ahmad Al-Bashir, is inconsistent with the constitution of the Republic of South Africa and invalid.

Voice
On Monday Judge President Dunston Mlambo condemned the government’s failure to prevent Sudanese president Omar al-Bashir’s departure from South Africa.
Al Bashir arrived in the country on Saturday for Sunday and Monday’s 25th African Union Summit.

Sound Up Erika
There was a lot of confusion at the African Union Summit whether he was attending,

Voice
By midday on Sunday a temporary high court order barred him from leaving the country.

Sound Up Angela Mudukuti
He’s been wanted since 2009, that’s the first time he was indicted. And again in 2010. So he is a fugitive.

Voice
Despite the court order on Sunday night his plane was reportedly moved to the Waterkloof Airforce base. Late on Monday morning as the case continued Al-Bashir was jetting home. The news of his departure reached Judge President Mlambo moments after he ordered the arrest and detainment of the Sudanese President

Voice
We met journalist Erika Gibson on a hill overlooking the Waterkloof Air Force Base. She followed President al-Bashir’s movements once he arrived in South Africa for the summit. A plane spotter friend picked up al-Bashir’s plane as it landed in Johannesburg at OR Tambo airport.

Sound Up Erika
And he sent me through the picture. So that again helped the whole court application and so on, they had proof that he was in the country.

Voice
Angela Mudukuti is an international criminal justice lawyer with the Southern African Litigation Center – a NGO that promotes human rights and the rule of law in the region. The same organization who took government to the North Gauteng High Court last week to have the arrest warrant against Omar al-Bashir enforced.

Sound Up Angela
This is what South Africa is obligated to do in terms of the law. Bashir was indicted by the ICC, South Africa domesticated the Rome Statute of the ICC in 2002, and committed to the fact that should a fugitive of justice be in South Africa he would be arrested.

Voice
But according to a report in the Mail and Guardian, President Jacob Zuma and his key security ministers plotted to ensure President Omar al-Bashir’s safe passage out of South Africa.

Sound Up Erika
It was about quarter to eleven that there was a whole flurry of activities, a huge convoy moved in under police escort, right straight to the plane, and it was cleared for take off. and shortly there after it took off.

Voice
Al-Bashir arrived back home in Sudan to huge fanfare. Speaking from the Sudanese capital Khartoum, Sudanese foreign minister Ibrahim al-Ghandour, dismissed the president’s close shave with international justice.

Sound Up Ibrahim al-Ghandour
We say that the international criminal court has been nearly completely ended in Africa by the refusal of all African states to implement its decisions.

Link John
It’s been more than 2000 days since the arrest warrant was issued for al-Bashir, but the question is why exactly is he a target for the ICC?

Voice
Omar al-Bashir came to power in Sudan following a coup in 1989, intensifying an ongoing war with the South of the Sudan that led to over 2 million deaths and the displacement of an estimated four million people.

Sound Up Andre Roux
It originated with a confluence of a humanitarian emergency situation with drought and conflict between the pastoralists, the nomadic herdsman, the so called Janjaweed, and the established farmers, the black Africans basically.



Voice
Andre Roux is a specialist intelligence and defense analyst, who has consulted for both the Institute for Security Studies and the International Criminal Court. He says the ongoing conflict in Darfur set the stage for the genocide that would start in 2003.

Sound Up Andre Roux
From that you had a ongoing civil war, the government used the Janjaweed as proxy militia forces, there’s credible evidence from the UN on that.

Sound Up Ahmed Abas
Every man over 15 years old is killed, and pregnant woman are cut open in case they are carrying a boy.

Voice
Ahmed Abas lived in Darfur when the genocide started, and fled to Chad when his village was attacked by the Janjaweed.

Sound Up Ahmed Abas
Sudan has become a country for Arabs only, and there is no room for blacks. The government wants to kill all the blacks, and replace them with Arabs, because Darfur land is good for cultivation.

Voice
Reports vary, but it is believed that between 300 and 400 000 men, women and children were killed during the Darfur genocide.

Sound Up Andre Roux
Andre: And the atrocities committed during this process you can link back to the chain of command, the commander in chief and the ministers involved. And this is where the war crime indictments have come from.
John: And the comaander in chief is al-Bashir?
Andre: al-Bashir.

Link John
In 2009 al-Bashir was invited to the inauguration of Jacob Zuma as president here at the Union Buildings, but he was told that if he arrived in this country he would likely face arrest. Fast forward six years and not only was he not threatened with arrest, he was given immunity from prosecution.

Sound Up Gwede Mantashe
You have South Africa hosting the AU summit, you say “arrest a head of state”, obviously when you take that decision you are contradicting the interest of the state versus judiciary, narrow judiciary.

Voice
ANC secretary general Gwede Mantashe says the party supports the state’s decision to allow President al-Bashir to attend the AU summit held in Johannesburg last week.

Sound Up Gwede
People forget that in this country we took a decision, consciously, not to arrest leaders of the Apartheid regime… Why should the judiciary today want to relegate South Africa into a pariah state in the continent?

Sound Up Angela
So our problem of course is that the government has acted in contravention of domestic law, contravention of international law, and in contravention of constitutional law by disobeying a court order.

Voice
And that is the crux of the matter, according to constitutional law expert Professor Pierre de Vos who spoke to us earlier this week from Italy, where he is away on business.

Sound Up Pierre de Vos
If this is repeated often enough, nobody will trust the legal system, because people will start believing that a court order wouldn’t be worth the paper it is written on.

Voice
While al-Bashir’s triumphant return home was seemingly celebrated by some of his people, it has left a sour taste in the mouths of many Sudanese refugees.

Sound Up Mohamed Isahq
This was really a very disappointing point for us as a population in Sudan, particularly in Darfur.

Voice
Mohamed Isahq is a Sudanese refugee who fled to Uganda during the genocide in Darfur. He says al-Bashir should not only be arrested for atrocities committed in the past, but also to protect the Sudanese people who are still on the ground in Darfur.

Sound Up Mohamed
I lost best friends and family members in this war which has taken place. And also currently I have all my family in an IDP camp where they live in conditions of the Janjaweed.

Link John
One of the criticisms of the ICC is that it disproportionately focuses on Africans. That’s a view echoed by the ANC which says the court has out lasted it’s usefulness.

Sound Up Gwede Mantashe
Nobody from developed countries has gone to that court, despite many many atrocities committed. Israel is not in that court, it has bombed Palestine everyday, nobody from Israel is in that court. Therefore that court is a tool of repression.

Voice
But South Africa and many other African states participated in the creation of the ICC .

Sound Up Angela
The majority of the cases before the ICC, those are what we call self referrals, where independent autonomous African governments have gone to the ICC and said we cannot handle this matter, can you investigate and then subsequently prosecute people.

Link John
While al-Bashir was facing arrest in this country, alarming reports started to emerge from Sudan. They suggested that a large contingent of Sudanese soldiers, who apparently were armed to the teeth, had gathered outside a military base housing South African peacekeepers.

Sound Up Erika
Now you’ve got your troops sitting there, and you’ve got a high drama playing off in South Africa.

Voice
Erika broke the story on Tuesday this week, having had contact with soldiers on the ground in Sudan.

Sound Up Erika
The guys started preparing themselves, you don’t know what the end result is going to be, so you prepare for the worst.

Voice
SANDF spokesperson Simphiwe Dlamini has denied the reports of our troops being under threat, and says it was business as usual in Darfur.

Sound Up Simphiwe Dlamini
We would want to clearly point out that at no stage were our members of the Defense Force under any threat. The troop movement did not affect us whatsoever and it was a movement that was going north of where we are, not even close to where we were.

Sound Up Erika
Erika: It was intimidation, and intimidation is part of the game in Sudan.

Voice
Whatever the rationale behind the al-Bashir fiasco, the South African government appears to have openly defied a High Court order; a move that professor de Vos warns could lead to a constitutional crisis.

Sound Up Pierre de Vos
We are not there yet, but of course if that happens the whole constitutional democracy collapses. In a constitutional democracy it is imperative of course that the government of the day should comply with court orders.

Voice
Meanwhile Judge President Dunston Mlambo has ordered the government to explain the circumstances surrounding al-Bashir’s flight from South Africa in an affidavit due in court this coming Tuesday – and it seems the ruling has left the ANC at loggerheads with the judiciary.

Sound Up Gwede
There is a drive in certain sections of the judiciary to create chaos for government, that’s our view. And we know it will happen in the Western Cape High court and it will happen in Gauteng. Those are the two benches where you see the narrative is totally negative and create a contradiction.

Sound Up Gwede People forget that in this country we took a decision, consciously, not to arrest leaders of the Apartheid regime… Why should the judiciary today want to relegate South Africa into a pariah state in the continent? Sound Up Angela So our problem of course is that the government has acted in contravention of domestic law, contravention of international law, and in contravention of constitutional law by disobeying a court order. Voice And that is the crux of the matter, according to constitutional law expert Professor Pierre de Vos who spoke to us earlier this week from Italy, where he is away on business. Sound Up Pierre de Vos If this is repeated often enough, nobody will trust the legal system, because people will start believing that a court order wouldn’t be worth the paper it is written on. Voice While al-Bashir’s triumphant return home was seemingly celebrated by some of his people, it has left a sour taste in the mouths of many Sudanese refugees. Sound Up Mohamed Isahq This was really a very disappointing point for us as a population in Sudan, particularly in Darfur. Voice Mohamed Isahq is a Sudanese refugee who fled to Uganda during the genocide in Darfur. He says al-Bashir should not only be arrested for atrocities committed in the past, but also to protect the Sudanese people who are still on the ground in Darfur. Sound Up Mohamed I lost best friends and family members in this war which has taken place. And also currently I have all my family in an IDP camp where they live in conditions of the Janjaweed. Link John One of the criticisms of the ICC is that it disproportionately focuses on Africans. That’s a view echoed by the ANC which says the court has out lasted it’s usefulness. Sound Up Gwede Mantashe Nobody from developed countries has gone to that court, despite many many atrocities committed. Israel is not in that court, it has bombed Palestine everyday, nobody from Israel is in that court. Therefore that court is a tool of repression. Voice But South Africa and many other African states participated in the creation of the ICC . Sound Up Angela The majority of the cases before the ICC, those are what we call self referrals, where independent autonomous African governments have gone to the ICC and said we cannot handle this matter, can you investigate and then subsequently prosecute people. Link John While al-Bashir was facing arrest in this country, alarming reports started to emerge from Sudan. They suggested that a large contingent of Sudanese soldiers, who apparently were armed to the teeth, had gathered outside a military base housing South African peacekeepers. Sound Up Erika Now you’ve got your troops sitting there, and you’ve got a high drama playing off in South Africa. Voice Erika broke the story on Tuesday this week, having had contact with soldiers on the ground in Sudan. Sound Up Erika The guys started preparing themselves, you don’t know what the end result is going to be, so you prepare for the worst. Voice SANDF spokesperson Simphiwe Dlamini has denied the reports of our troops being under threat, and says it was business as usual in Darfur. Sound Up Simphiwe Dlamini We would want to clearly point out that at no stage were our members of the Defense Force under any threat. The troop movement did not affect us whatsoever and it was a movement that was going north of where we are, not even close to where we were. Sound Up Erika Erika: It was intimidation, and intimidation is part of the game in Sudan. Voice Whatever the rationale behind the al-Bashir fiasco, the South African government appears to have openly defied a High Court order; a move that professor de Vos warns could lead to a constitutional crisis. Sound Up Pierre de Vos We are not there yet, but of course if that happens the whole constitutional democracy collapses. In a constitutional democracy it is imperative of course that the government of the day should comply with court orders. Voice Meanwhile Judge President Dunston Mlambo has ordered the government to explain the circumstances surrounding al-Bashir’s flight from South Africa in an affidavit due in court this coming Tuesday – and it seems the ruling has left the ANC at loggerheads with the judiciary. Sound Up Gwede There is a drive in certain sections of the judiciary to create chaos for government, that’s our view. And we know it will happen in the Western Cape High court and it will happen in Gauteng. Those are the two benches where you see the narrative is totally negative and create a contradiction.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As international condemnation floods in about the al-Bashir incident, we ask if government's blatant disregard of a high court order is the first step to a full blown constitutional crisis.
metadata.Summary: With the South African government seemingly complicit in allowing a high profile fugitive from justice to escape our borders, we examine the consequences of the ruling party's decision to blatantly disregard both international and local laws. In the meantime, reports are circulating that SA troops were basically threatened and or held hostage in Sudan during al-Bashir's visit to SA. But should the interests of SA's relationships with it's African counterparts trump the rule of law?
